title: Properties of Bulk Matter
tagline: How matter behaves in bulk: elasticity, fluid pressure, viscosity, surface tension and Bernoulli's principle.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI Physics syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Syllabus unit and chapter title were taken from the official-verified ISC Physics registry entry; no board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Gases and liquids are often treated as fluids because they both flow, but matter in bulk shows a wider range of behaviour than flow alone. A solid can stretch or compress a little and then return to shape, or it can deform permanently. A liquid can exert pressure on the base and sides of a container, resist motion through internal friction, and draw itself together at a free surface. A moving fluid can trade speed for pressure in ways that are surprisingly useful, from atomisers to aircraft wings. This chapter brings those properties together: elasticity, fluid pressure, viscosity, surface tension and Bernoulli's principle.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Elasticity and Hooke's law; Young's modulus; fluid pressure and variation with depth; viscosity and Stokes' law; surface tension and capillary rise; Bernoulli's principle and its applications

learningOutcomes: Distinguish elastic deformation from plastic deformation.
State Hooke's law and explain the meaning of Young's modulus.
Explain how pressure in a fluid varies with depth.
Describe viscosity as internal friction in fluids and give examples.
Explain surface tension in terms of molecular forces and describe capillary rise.
State Bernoulli's principle and apply it to simple situations.
Connect each phenomenon to a real effect rather than only a definition.

blocks.text: When a suitable force is applied to a solid, it may change shape or size. If the solid returns to its original shape when the force is removed, the deformation is called elastic. If it does not return completely, the deformation is plastic. Elasticity is not the same as strength: a material can be elastic and still break if the force is too large. The simplest elastic behaviour is described by Hooke's law, which says that for small deformations the restoring force is proportional to the extension or compression, provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded.

items: Elastic deformation is recovered when the deforming force is removed.
Plastic deformation is permanent.
Hooke's law applies only within the limit of proportionality.
Young's modulus is the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain in a wire or rod.
A larger Young's modulus means a stiffer material for the same cross-section.

items.text: A steel spring can be stretched and returns to its shape because it is elastic, while modelling clay keeps the shape you give it because it deforms plastically. Both are solids, but their bulk behaviour is different.
items.note: The distinction is about recovery after the force is removed.

blocks.text: A fluid at rest exerts pressure on the walls of its container and on any object immersed in it. Pressure in a fluid increases with depth because the fluid above adds weight. In a liquid of constant density, the pressure at a point is greater the deeper it is. This is why a dam is built thicker at the base than at the top, and why ears feel pressure when a diver goes down. Pressure in a fluid at rest acts equally in all directions at the same depth.

items: Pressure is force per unit area.
In a stationary fluid, pressure increases with depth.
At the same depth in a connected fluid, pressure is the same in all directions.
Atmospheric pressure acts on free surfaces and must often be taken into account.
A barometer measures atmospheric pressure; a manometer compares pressures.

items.text: If two holes are made in the side of a water bottle, one near the top and one near the bottom, the lower jet travels farther because the pressure at the lower hole is greater.
items.note: The difference is not magic; it is the weight of the water above each hole.

blocks.text: Viscosity is the internal friction in a fluid that opposes relative motion between layers. Honey is more viscous than water because it resists flow more strongly. Viscosity is why a sphere falling through a fluid does not accelerate forever: the fluid exerts a drag that increases with speed. For a small sphere at low speeds, Stokes' law gives the viscous drag in terms of the fluid's viscosity, the sphere's radius and its speed. When the downward weight is balanced by the sum of the viscous drag and the buoyant force, the sphere reaches a constant terminal velocity.

items: Viscosity is a measure of a fluid's resistance to flow.
Higher viscosity means greater internal friction.
A sphere falling in a fluid can reach a steady terminal velocity.
Stokes' law applies for small spheres and slow flow.
Temperature affects viscosity: liquids usually become less viscous when heated.

items.text: A raindrop does not accelerate indefinitely as it falls; at some speed the upward drag and buoyancy together balance the weight, and the drop falls at a steady terminal velocity.
items.note: Terminal velocity is the result of competing forces, not a property of the drop alone.

blocks.text: The free surface of a liquid behaves somewhat like a stretched membrane. This effect is called surface tension. It arises because molecules just inside the surface are pulled inward by neighbouring molecules, so the surface tends to minimise its area. Surface tension explains why small droplets are nearly spherical, why a carefully placed steel needle can float on water, and why soap helps water spread and wet fabrics. In a narrow tube, surface tension together with the contact angle can cause the liquid to rise or fall; this is capillary action.

items: Surface tension is due to unbalanced molecular attractions at the surface.
It tends to minimise the surface area of a liquid.
It produces the spherical shape of small droplets.
Capillary rise occurs in narrow tubes when the liquid wets the walls.
Detergents reduce surface tension and improve wetting and cleaning.

items.text: Water in a clean glass capillary tube rises because water wets glass; mercury in a similar tube is depressed because it does not wet glass in the same way.
items.note: Capillary action depends on the interaction between the liquid and the solid surface, not just on surface tension alone.

blocks.text: Bernoulli's principle links the speed, pressure and height of a moving fluid, assuming steady flow and some simplifying conditions. In simple terms, where the speed of a fluid is higher, the pressure is lower, and vice versa, if height differences are taken into account. This is a powerful idea because it explains several effects that at first seem unrelated: why a sheet of paper rises when air is blown across its top, why a fluid speeds up when it passes through a narrow section of pipe, and how the shape of a wing can contribute to lift.

items: Bernoulli's principle follows from conservation of energy in a moving fluid.
For a given fluid stream, higher speed is associated with lower pressure.
The principle applies simply only when the flow is steady and losses are small.
The narrower the cross-section, the faster the fluid tends to move.
Applications include atomisers, Venturi tubes and the effect of shape on lift.

items.text: Hold two sheets of paper parallel and a little apart, and blow air into the gap between them. They move closer rather than apart, because the moving air between them lowers the pressure there.
items.note: This is a simple demonstration of the speed-pressure connection, not a full account of why wings lift.

keyPoints: Bulk matter behaves by elasticity, fluid pressure, viscosity, surface tension and flow effects.
Elastic solids return to shape; plastic solids do not.
Hooke's law works only up to the limit of proportionality.
Young's modulus measures stiffness for tensile deformation.
Fluid pressure increases with depth and acts in all directions at a given depth.
Viscosity is internal friction; it leads to terminal velocity in falling objects.
Surface tension makes small droplets spherical and causes capillary rise or fall.
Bernoulli's principle links speed, pressure and height in a moving fluid.
examFocus: When a question asks about elasticity, be clear whether it is asking about the idea of elasticity, Hooke's law or a modulus such as Young's modulus.
For Bernoulli's principle, do not use it as a universal explanation; state its conditions and use it only where they are reasonable.
In fluid questions, distinguish between pressure, force and density instead of using the words interchangeably.

vocabulary.meaning: The ability of a body to regain its original shape after the deforming force is removed.
The relation, within limits, that strain is proportional to stress.
The ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain; a measure of stiffness.
A fluid's internal resistance to flow.
The effect that makes a liquid surface behave like a stretched membrane.
The rise of a liquid in a narrow tube due to surface tension and wetting.
The relation between speed, pressure and height in a moving fluid.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a perfectly elastic deformation is correct?
options: The body returns to its original shape when the force is removed
It can occur only in liquids
It does not depend on the force at all
questions.answer: The body returns to its original shape when the force is removed
questions.explanation: Elastic deformation is recovered after the deforming force is removed.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking that any stretching is elastic regardless of whether the body returns.

questions.prompt: Young's modulus is the ratio of:
questions.explanation: Young's modulus is defined as tensile stress divided by tensile strain in the elastic region.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing stress with strain or mixing up the definition with force/area alone.

questions.prompt: Why does pressure in a liquid at rest increase with depth?
questions.answer: Because the liquid above a point has weight, so the deeper point supports more fluid above it, and weight of fluid produces pressure.
questions.explanation: The increase with depth comes from the weight of the fluid overhead.
questions.commonMistake: Saying pressure increases with depth for no physical reason, or because of the container's shape alone.

questions.prompt: What is terminal velocity, and what forces are involved when a sphere falls through a fluid?
questions.answer: Terminal velocity is the constant speed reached when the downward force of weight is balanced by the upward buoyant force and the viscous drag from the fluid.
questions.explanation: The sphere no longer accelerates because the net force is zero.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking the object stops accelerating because it runs out of force, rather than because forces balance.

questions.prompt: Explain why the pressure at a given depth in a liquid does not depend on the shape of the container.
questions.answer: Pressure in a liquid at rest depends on depth and density, not on the shape or total amount of liquid. At a given depth, the weight of the liquid column above the point determines the extra pressure, and if the vertical depth is the same, the pressure is the same, regardless of whether the container is wide, narrow or oddly shaped.
questions.explanation: Pressure at a point in a stationary fluid is a function of depth, not of the container's overall form.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming a larger container must automatically have a larger pressure at the same depth.
